idiom_name: struct holding HashMap plus a &mut self method
implementation_notes: Rust has no memoize wrapper in the standard library, so the honest form is a struct that owns the cache: a HashMap field and a method that takes &mut self, checks get(), computes on a miss and inserts the result. Recursion then goes through the method itself, which is why the struct is not just a style choice - a closure cannot capture itself, so recursive memoization is unwritable as a closure and the explicit cache parameter (or struct) is the pattern's justified classic form. For interior mutability in a shared context, wrap the map in Mutex/RwLock (or RefCell for single-threaded code); the compiler enforces the choice, since RefCell is not Sync and a closure holding one cannot cross threads.
pitfalls: The method needs &mut self, so a Memo cannot be called through a shared reference; sharing it across threads requires Mutex<HashMap> and an explicit lock, not a bigger struct.
RefCell is not Sync, so a RefCell-backed cache in a closure cannot be sent across threads - the compiler error is the design check, not an obstacle to work around.
Recursive memoization as a self-referential closure does not compile in safe Rust; restructure to the struct or pass the cache as a parameter.
An unbounded HashMap retains every key and value for the owner's lifetime; bound the domain or add an LRU store for long-running processes.

variants.name: OnceLock / LazyLock for a single value
variants.implementation_notes: For the nullary case the standard library does provide the facility: OnceLock (stable since 1.70) is a thread-safe cell written once, and get_or_init guarantees that many threads may call it concurrently yet only one initializer runs, which is exactly the memo guarantee for a value that has no arguments; LazyLock is the same idea with the initializer attached and derefs like &T. The documented trap is re-entrancy - it is an error to initialise the cell from inside its own initializer, and the current implementation deadlocks while the outcome is explicitly unspecified - so the initializer must not call back into the same cell. Single-threaded code can use std::cell::OnceCell instead, and anything keyed by arguments still needs a map plus a lock or a cache crate.
pitfalls: Reentrant initialisation deadlocks (documented as unspecified behaviour with the current implementation); never touch the cell from its own initializer.
A panic inside the initializer leaves the cell uninitialized and propagates, so the next caller retries a failing computation.
OnceLock covers only the zero-argument case: turning it into an argument-keyed memo means a map inside the cell and a lock around it.
A static cell holds its value for the program's lifetime, including everything the value references.

variants.name: #[cached] attribute macro (cached crate)
variants.implementation_notes: The practical route for argument-keyed memoization is the cached crate's attribute macro: #[cached] wraps the function body with a store keyed on the arguments, #[cached(max_size = N)] adds an LRU bound, ttl_secs adds expiry, and #[once] covers the nullary case. The crate's documentation is explicit about the concurrency default - #[cached] has no write synchronization, so concurrent uncached calls for the same key may each compute independently and overwrite each other, matching the stdlib decorators of other languages - while sync_writes = by_key deduplicates them at the price of per-key locks that must not be used on recursive or re-entrant functions. That makes the crate the right default for a service-shaped memo and the wrong one for a deeply recursive function, where the explicit struct below stays clearer.
pitfalls: The default has no write synchronization (documented), so identical concurrent misses can duplicate the computation; sync_writes = by_key deduplicates but must not annotate recursive functions (deadlock).
Arguments must be Clone and Hash, and the macro stores the key, so large argument structs become part of the retained footprint.
Option and Result returns are treated specially (None/Err are not cached by default), which is usually desirable and occasionally surprising.
The store lives for the program's lifetime unless a bound is configured, so a TTL or max_size belongs on every unbounded key domain.
